Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. It’s... well, it’s a little hard to articulate, which is ironic given my line of work, but what finally brought me in today is that I just feel like... like the part of me that used to reach for people has gone completely quiet. 

I’m a social worker, you see—mental health and substance abuse—so my entire career, my whole adult life really, since grad school, has been built on connecting with others and really investing in their well-being. And I used to genuinely take so much pleasure in that. I took pleasure in a lot of things, actually. I was always doing yoga to stay grounded, going to art galleries on the weekends just to be around creativity and color, and I used to write pages and pages in my journals. I have stacks of them at home, filled with thoughts and reflections. 

But lately... I don't know, I look at my journal and I just feel nothing. There's no spark to pick up the pen. I don't care about the galleries, the yoga mat just gathers dust, and even at work, I’m mostly just moving through obligations. I show up, I do the paperwork, I sit with the clients and go through the motions, but the joy, the actual feeling of being alive and engaged in my life... it’s just gone. It’s all so incredibly flat and silent inside my head. I wake up and I just do what I have to do because I have to do it, not because I want to. And I just thought, I can’t keep living on this kind of empty autopilot forever, you know?

Well, I’ve actually spent a lot of time trying to pinpoint the exact timeline, because, you know, in my line of work I’m always asking my own clients to look for the catalyst or the starting point of their distress. And looking back, this whole change in how I’m thinking, how I'm working, and how I'm connecting—or failing to connect—with people... it’s been going on for about eight months. 

It really all started right around the time we took my older relative into our apartment. Which, as you can imagine, was a pretty massive adjustment. I mean, we live in an apartment, so space is already at a premium, and suddenly we had to rearrange our entire lives, our routines, the physical layout of our home just to accommodate them. It was one of those family obligations where you can't exactly say no, so you just do it. But my home used to be my sanctuary, the place where I could decompress, roll out my yoga mat, and really process my day. 

At first, I just chalked it up to caregiver burnout or just the sheer exhaustion of the transition. I figured I was just tired from moving their things and getting them settled. But then a month went by, and then three months, and now here we are eight months later, and they're fully settled in, but I never bounced back. The exhaustion just sort of morphed into this deep, pervasive emptiness. So yes, about eight months of just feeling entirely disconnected from the life I built.

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Sleep. You'd think with how completely drained and flat I feel all day, I'd just be sleeping all the time, right? But honestly... I haven't really noticed any major changes in my sleep. I mean, I still go to bed around the same time I always have, usually after I finish up my charting for the day or after I’ve sort of just sat in the living room for a while, staring at the wall instead of reading or journaling like I used to. I know sometimes when people get depressed or burnt out—and I see this all the time with my clients—they either can't sleep at all, they're up pacing the floors until three in the morning, or they can't drag themselves out of bed and they're sleeping fourteen hours a day. But for me, it's just... normal, I guess? Or as normal as it can be when everything else feels so wrong. I get my seven or eight hours. I'm not lying awake agonizing over things, because, well, I don't really have the energy to agonize over anything anymore. There's no anxiety keeping me up, no racing thoughts. It's just quiet. 

So, yeah, my sleep hasn't really been the issue. It's the waking hours that are the problem. It's getting out of that bed after a perfectly adequate night of sleep and just feeling absolutely nothing about the day ahead. I almost wish I was having trouble sleeping, because then at least I'd have something tangible to point to, you know? A reason for why I feel this way. But no, sleep has been pretty much the same as it was before all this started.

Worthlessness or guilt? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know what that looks like. I sit across from clients all day long who are drowning in guilt over things they couldn't possibly control, or who feel completely worthless because they lost a job or a relationship ended. I know I'm a responsible person. I took in my older relative when they needed a place to stay, and I managed that whole transition, which was a massive undertaking, as I mentioned. I just sit around feeling nothing. There's no inner critic screaming at me that I'm useless. It's just silence. So, no, I haven't been struggling with guilt or feeling worthless. I just don't feel much of anything, which, honestly, is almost more frustrating because there's nothing to fight against. When a client feels worthless, we can work on challenging those cognitive distortions, we can look for evidence to the contrary. But how do you challenge a complete lack of feeling? There's no distortion to correct, just a void. So, no guilt, no worthlessness. Just this pervasive, flat emptiness.

Sadness? Hmm. No, I wouldn't use that word. I mean, sadness is an active emotion, isn't it? It has a weight to it, a distinct presence. When you're sad, you feel it—you feel it in your throat, or behind your eyes, or like a heavy pressure sitting right on your chest. 

I see people all day long who are profoundly sad. They sit on the couch in my office and they weep, they go through half a box of tissues in forty-five minutes, they talk about this crushing despair they just can't shake. I know what sadness looks like, and I know what it feels like from earlier points in my life. But right now? No. I haven't shed a tear in... well, I honestly couldn't even tell you the last time I cried. 

It’s actually kind of strange, because there are things happening in my life that objectively *should* make me sad, or at least a little melancholy. Like my older relative moving in with me—the whole reason that happened is because their health has significantly declined. They can't live independently anymore. And I look at them sometimes, struggling just to get out of the armchair in the living room, and I know, logically, as a human being, this is a sad situation. This is the physical decline of someone I've known my whole life. But internally? I don't feel that pang of sorrow. I don't feel any grief about it. I just register it as a factual data point: "They are struggling to stand up. I need to make sure the walker is positioned closer to the chair next time." It's entirely functional. It's completely operational. 

Even at work, last week I had a termination session with a client I've been seeing for three years. It was a beautiful wrap-up, they had finally reconciled with their estranged daughter, which was our main treatment goal. Normally, a session like that would bring a tear to my eye, or I'd at least feel a deep warmth and a sense of moving emotion. But I just sat there, observing it like I was watching a documentary on television. No sadness that it was ending, no joy for their progress. Just... neutral observation. 

So, no, no crying spells, no feeling blue or down in the dumps, no hopelessness. Hopelessness implies you desperately want things to get better but you don't think they will. I don't have that desperation. Sadness would almost be a relief, honestly, because at least it's a feeling. At least it means your emotional receptors are still firing. But no, I haven't been feeling sad. Just perfectly, consistently flat.

Medical conditions? Like thyroid issues? No, no, nothing like that. Like I've somehow stepped outside the room, or stepped outside of myself, and they're waiting for the real me to come back and explain what just happened. But I don't have an explanation. I just quickly scramble the pens or apologize and pretend I was just clearing my throat, and I try to force myself to sit perfectly still for the rest of the meeting. It's just so bizarre, and it's so unlike me. I've always been so composed, so professional, and now I'm sitting there playing with office supplies and echoing people like a parrot. It's very unsettling.
